article.title: What I Learned in Nagasaki
article.author: Chuck Yates
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. One day in 1964, at the age of nineteen, I rode around Nagasaki on a tour bus with a Japanese friend. Profoundly ignorant of Japan, I was ill equipped to process the sights we saw—the broken ruins of Urakami Cathedral, near the hypocenter, and the peace park with its monumental statue sitting atop the hill, right hand pointing to the sky as if warning of danger from above, left hand extended palm down as if urging peace and harmony, eyes closed as if in prayer. Nor was I prepared for the city’s A-bomb museum. In one room, there was a section of the wooden outer wall of a building, unremarkable except for the human silhouette burned into it. As I stood there trying to take in what I was seeing, I realized I was surrounded by Japanese people speaking softly to each other. I had no idea what they were saying, but it dawned on me that I was the only American in a room full of Japanese looking at exhibits of the horrors other Americans had inflicted on their city. Terrified, I fled and cowered in the back of the bus, knowing that all those Japanese would be getting back on, that my friend would be getting back on, and wondering how I would face them. I realized, eventually, that I was not personally responsible for what other Americans had done. But I realized also that I was not off the hook, that it was my responsibility to do whatever I could to help make sure nothing like that ever happened again. Related: Controlling Unalienable Rights in Idaho It’s been over eighty years since the United States used nuclear weapons against people. About 80,000 died instantly in Hiroshima, another 40,000 in Nagasaki, some leaving nothing behind but their shadows. In the following weeks, that many more died slowly from burns and radiation poisoning. And by the time the nukes fell, US bombers had already destroyed most of the other cities in Japan. In a single night in Tokyo, incendiary bombs caused a fire storm that killed a hundred thousand. For many years, I taught at a college where we took K-12 educators to Japan, and we always took them to Hiroshima. When they emerged from the museum, some were white-faced and silent, others weeping openly. And some were telling each other, “That’s nothing compared to what Hitler did to the Jews,” or “After what they did to us at Pearl Harbor, they had it coming.” Some visitors will face the horrors they see. Others will equivocate, unwilling to accept the reality of what ordinary and fundamentally decent people are capable of doing to each other. Most Americans these days know little or nothing about the American destruction of Japan. It's not part of their lived experience, and more recent horrors have taken stage front: the devastation of 9/11, the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, the death toll from the pandemic, the seizure of Venezuela, the ongoing war with Iran, and the president’s cavalier trivialization of the suffering he has caused. Related: The National Anthem and America's Dangerous Brand of Patriotism Many turn away in the knowledge that they can do nothing to stop the human tragedy they witness, or maybe they just hope to duck another blow to their exhausted sensibilities. Yet it seems to me we have an obligation at least to be aware, to know what our leaders are doing in our name, if not actually to stand up and challenge them. The First Amendment remains in effect, despite the willingness of so many to ignore it. As you read these words, immigrants are being hunted across the country in defiance of both law and decency, caged like animals, brutalized, dehumanized, and deported to whatever fate awaits them. And as you read these words, Iranians and Palestinians are dying from relentless American and Israeli violence, or searching through the rubble of their ruined cities for missing family and friends, wondering what they have done to provoke our hostility. We think of ourselves a city on a hill, and we tell ourselves that people everywhere look to us as their best hope for freedom and dignity. Yet when they come to us in search of the better lives our founding documents promise them, or when they remain faithful to their own beliefs, we call them enemies and perpetrate atrocity on them. And we equivocate, unwilling to accept the reality of what ordinary and fundamentally decent people are capable of doing to each other.
